approach.method_basis: The Parent evolves molecular graphs from a bounded population of accepted high-scoring molecules. Score-quantile parent sampling, connected-fragment crossover and local graph mutations create a fresh surplus pool. It retains stable canonical identity admission and a formula-preserving aromatic nitrogen-position exchange. A Gaussian process trained on every earlier accepted score predicts the pool using binary local-environment fingerprints, and correlated posterior draws choose evaluations. Feedback updates both the breeding population and the full prediction archive. Its posterior always uses the same small standardized noise scale, regardless of disagreement between molecular similarity and the accepted scores.
approach.novelty: Learn that one noise scale from the current accepted archive. At each fit, compare a fixed small ladder of noise scales by Gaussian marginal likelihood and condition the existing posterior with the best-supported value. This lets observed score relationships determine how strongly the model interpolates nearby molecules and how much uncertainty remains. The earlier posterior sibling changed binary environment presence to counts while retaining fixed noise; this experiment keeps the Parent representation and tests feedback-dependent regularization as a separate mechanism. Earlier graph and parent-allocation mechanisms remain inherited.

hypothesis: Select the Gaussian process observation-noise scale at each fit by accepted-archive marginal likelihood over a fixed ladder around the inherited scale, so task-local label agreement controls posterior regularization.

finding_summary.headline: Learned noise improved selected-stream error and coverage, but mean search score fell 0.015961
finding_summary.insights: The experiment separates a real regularization benefit from a search benefit. The strongest controlled prediction improvement occurs in sitagliptin: latent coverage rises from 466 to 558 of 870 scored molecules, with lower MSE in all three seeds. DRD2 instead loses three covered molecules on the same scored identities, and ranking deteriorates in the pooled comparison. Thus reducing average prediction error and winning training likelihood do not establish better discrimination among the next candidates to evaluate. The frequent upper and lower boundary choices show that different accepted molecular/score relationships call for very different regularization; they leave the adequacy of the finite ladder unresolved. Substantial undercoverage remains even with learned noise, particularly in the harder streams. Scalar noise cannot distinguish molecules with identical binary fingerprints or correct every mismatch in the representation and mean model. The chemical assessment also finds recurring ring-rich families with more reactive N/O-halogen and peroxide motifs, oversized assemblies and unresolved stereochemistry, so these predictive gains supply no evidence that chemical liabilities were repaired. The measured same-data comparison supports a modest, heterogeneous prediction benefit. It cannot assign counterfactual scores to unselected molecules or identify which changed choices caused the loss in whole-search endpoints. The mechanism executed; the expected score improvement did not occur.
finding_summary.results: Noise selection changed the implemented posterior in 434 of 435 fits, and every likelihood winner and recorded evaluation choice reconstructed correctly. The smallest available noise won 179 fits and the largest won 116; the chosen scale changed after feedback at 41 of 420 opportunities. On the same earlier archives and the same 4350 subsequently scored molecules, prediction MSE fell from 0.0121771 with fixed noise to 0.0116233 with learned noise. Latent 95% interval coverage rose from 79.75% to 82.51%, while mean within-batch rank correlation fell from 0.41596 to 0.39609. Noise-inclusive coverage reached 89.91% with wider intervals, reported separately from latent uncertainty. The same random draws applied to the two distributions changed the selected molecule set in 255 of 435 batches. Despite those prediction gains, mean final-best score fell from 0.551771 to 0.535810, a paired change of -0.015961 against the registered +0.002 target; seed variability increased from 0.008223 to 0.023346. One seed macro improved and two declined. Task means rose for median and sitagliptin and slightly for decoration, but fell for DRD2 and zaleplon. All tasks completed their budgets, and every factorization succeeded at the first jitter.

molecular.headline: Ring-rich molecules retain reactive substituents, oversized assemblies and unresolved stereochemistry
molecular.overall_character: This assessment covers every supplied trajectory for node n-9002c3d22369 and parent n-9edaa26007c3: all five objectives and seeds 0, 1 and 2, with 900 observations and 870 optimizer proposals per objective in each node. The digest's tasks_without_trajectories list is empty. Its initial excerpt represents seed 0 and its final excerpt represents seed 2; the full trajectories were read to cover the other seeds. The molecules contain abundant phenyl and aza-aromatic rings, fused and bridged heterocycles, carbonyl groups, ethers, amines and halogens. Different seeds retain different families, including indole carboxamides, thiocarbonyl-linked pyrazoles, repeated carbonyl-bearing heteroaryls, aryl-linked cyclic amines and annulated dicarbonyl heterocycles. Structural diversity is moderate across the panel but uneven within the stronger examples. SMILES uniqueness alone would overstate chemically useful diversity. The digest's ring-closure rates range from 0.9609 to 0.9908 and aromatic-token presence rates from 0.9460 to 0.9908; these are fractions of proposal strings, not atom fractions or perceived ring counts. Passive RDKit 2023.09.6 parsing succeeds for all 4350 generated records per node. The child has a median of 31 heavy atoms, 5 perceived rings and 3 aromatic rings; the parent has 30, 5 and 3. Child N-halogen-bearing, O-halogen-bearing and O-O-bearing molecule counts are 870, 375 and 161, compared with 667, 319 and 85 in the parent. These structural alerts require chemical context: a valid graph is not a synthesis or stability demonstration, and an N-S bond by itself is not an objection. Some conventional aromatic amides and amine scaffolds look tractable, but the repeated reactive groups and large or unusually connected ring systems make overall synthetic plausibility questionable and drug-likeness weak. Every generated SMILES is formally uncharged and lacks specified tetrahedral or double-bond stereochemistry; RDKit identifies unassigned tetrahedral centres in 2200 child molecules. Basic amines nevertheless occur prominently, so the charge encoding does not establish solution-state neutrality. All score statements below reuse observed labels; no new molecular scoring, activation judgement, synthesis calculation or target-specific pharmacophore inference was performed. Numeric graph descriptions, full file hashes and seed comparisons are reproducible from /projects/standard/adeshwal/shared/zhou2577/SPIRAL/runs/SPIRAL2/policy/responses/r0011-08-improve-L01-molecular-audit.json and its adjacent passive audit script.

per_task.generated_character: These are mainly compact ring-rich heteroaromatics: the proposal median is 25 heavy atoms. Seed 0's stronger family contains phenolic pyrazoles with thiocarbonyl linkers and small unsaturated carbocycles, including a cyclobutenol and a cyclopentadiene in its best molecule. Seeds 1 and 2 favour alkoxy/alkyl-substituted indoles bearing pyridyl carboxamides. Each seed's best molecule has 25 heavy atoms; seed 0 has 4 perceived rings, while seeds 1 and 2 have 3. The seed-1 best retains a conventional secondary amide with carbon-bound halogens; the seed-2 best instead has an N-F amide. The latter remains a recognisable medicinal scaffold but has a chemically consequential substituent on its amide nitrogen. Later seed-2 molecules also contain rearranged annulated N/O ring systems, thiocarbonyls and O-F bonds. The digest records ring-closure presence 0.9770, aromatic-token presence 0.9598 and halogen presence 0.7598.
liabilities: N-F amides occur among the highest-scoring molecules, and 258 of 870 proposals have an N-halogen bond. The conventional secondary amide in the cited seed-1 best shows that useful observed scores can coexist with a more ordinary linkage.

The cyclobutenol/thiocarbonyl family and later heavily annulated structures raise stability, strain and synthetic-route questions. O-F-bearing late products and tiny oxidising or halogen fragments further show that sanitisation does not enforce ordinary medicinal chemistry.
missing_features: The supported opportunity is a wider set of compact heteroatom and carbonyl arrangements with intact ordinary amide connectivity. The stronger examples remain concentrated in the indole/carboxamide and pyrazole/thiocarbonyl families; these trajectories do not identify an absent target-specific ring or substituent.

Chemically resolved stereoisomers are absent even for the cyclobutenol-containing high scorer. This is missing structural definition; the supplied score comparisons do not establish a stereochemical reward.

The initial trimethoxy indole carboxamide scores 0.3051048083696145; the cited substituted pyridyl/indole N-F amide reaches 0.4387992465191. per_task.generated_character: This is the largest and most aromatic output family: the proposal median is 69 heavy atoms, 9 perceived rings and 8 aromatic rings, with a maximum of 120 heavy atoms. The digest's mean SMILES length is 124.8 and both ring-closure and aromatic-token presence are 0.9908. Seed 0 forms large aza-aromatic assemblies with imines, carbonyl linkers, vinyl ethers and annulated rings. Seed 1 forms long linked phenyl/aza-aryl and carbonyl-bearing O/N heteroaromatic assemblies, decorated with alkoxy groups, imines, nitriles and chloromethyl ethers. Its best molecule has 84 heavy atoms and 8 aromatic rings and includes an allene. Seed 2 remains smaller, around a median of 39 heavy atoms, but repeats N-methyl dicarbonyl fused heterocycles around an aza-aryl linker and frequently carries N-F groups. Its digest-final examples also show N-Cl and O-Cl. These are elaborate heteroatom-rich structures, with limited evidence of practical synthetic accessibility.
liabilities: Very high ring and atom counts create substantial synthetic and physicochemical burden. Chloromethyl ethers, imines, allene or conjugated enol-ether-like sections and, in the other seed family, N-F/N-Cl/O-Cl groups add distinct reactivity concerns.

None of the proposed alkene or imine arrangements has specified double-bond stereochemistry. Repeated, nearly equally scored large structures do not establish a well-defined or tractable decoration pattern.
missing_features: Compact alternatives that retain the useful heteroaromatic/carbonyl arrangement without repeating entire ring-rich fragments are underrepresented among the highest labels. The smaller seed-2 family shows useful scores without the largest assemblies, but no matched deletion experiment establishes how much can be removed.

The supplied molecules do not reveal an absent required decoration or reference scaffold. What is visibly missing is reliable structural economy and chemically ordinary substituent coverage around the recurring O/N heteroaromatic motifs.

per_task.generated_character: These molecules contain substantial saturated nitrogen chemistry alongside aryl groups: the proposal medians are 36 heavy atoms, 5 perceived rings and 2 aromatic rings. Seed 0's stronger products combine substituted aryl groups, small N-containing rings and an unusual sulfur centre written with S-H and S=N connectivity. Seed 1 contains more annulated saturated/partially unsaturated N-heterocycles with an aryl sulfoxide. Seed 2's best has 31 heavy atoms, two phenyl rings and an aminopyrrolidine, together with an amidine, a secondary amine/methylene-diamine linkage, a methylamino substituent, phenol and aryl bromide. Accessible basic centres are abundant in this family. All structures are nevertheless encoded without formal charge. The digest records halogen presence 0.9931; 854 of 870 proposals have an unassigned tetrahedral centre in the passive RDKit reading.
liabilities: The sulfur-containing high scorers combine S-H/S=N/N-S connectivity with strained small N-containing rings; no route, stability or three-dimensional geometry was supplied for them.

The amine/amidine-rich high scorer may have multiple ionisation possibilities, but no pKa or protonation-state analysis was performed. Unspecified stereochemistry, dense halogenation and occasional O-halogen bonds further limit the meaning of an apparently favourable scalar label.
missing_features: The aryl/basic-nitrogen arrangement is present, but its stereochemistry and alternative ionisation states are not represented. The highest-scoring seed-2 molecule has unassigned stereocentres despite several potentially basic sites; the trajectory does not establish which state or isomer would score better.

Chemically ordinary alternatives to the unusual sulfur and aminal connections are incompletely represented in the stronger families. The observations support studying the spacing and integrity of existing aryl/amine motifs, not inventing a required target-specific substituent.

per_task.generated_character: The output centres on medium-sized carbonyl-rich polycycles: the proposal median is 31 heavy atoms, with 5 perceived rings and 3 aromatic rings. Halogen presence is only 0.1586 in the digest, while ring-closure and aromatic-token presence are 0.9908 and 0.9839. Seed 0 combines aza-aryl/phenyl groups with an expanded dicarbonyl nitrogen heterocycle; seed 1 generates intertwined cyclic ether, lactam and urea-like ring systems; seed 2 retains aza-aryl-linked fused/bridged dicarbonyl N-heterocycles. The best seed-1 molecule has 35 heavy atoms and 5 rings, of which 2 are aromatic, and includes an eight-membered heterocycle and an N/O-substituted acetal-like carbon. There is real partial saturation and ring-topology variation, with many recognisable functional groups, but the precise annulations and stereochemistry make synthetic plausibility uncertain.

There are 477 generated molecules with unassigned tetrahedral centres and no assigned centres. The stream also contains O-O-bearing products, although the cited stronger examples largely avoid the N-halogen motifs prominent elsewhere.
missing_features: The stronger examples still cover a limited set of annulated dicarbonyl families. Alternative ring connections that reposition the existing N/O groups at comparable size are an evident coverage gap; no unseen reference-specific motif can be identified from the modest labels alone.

The acetal-containing and other potentially stereogenic ring systems lack stereochemical definition. The output demonstrates partial saturation, but does not demonstrate controlled stereoisomer or conformational coverage.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Among 4350 generated child molecules, 870 contain N-halogen bonds, 375 contain O-halogen bonds and 161 contain O-O bonds; the corresponding parent counts are 667, 319 and 85. Digest-cited strong examples include an N-F carboxamide, N-fluorinated dicarbonyl heterocycles and a terminal N-S(H) group, while ordinary secondary amides also attain useful observed labels.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator does not reliably preserve ordinary functional-group chemistry when changing local atom and bond environments.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Support chemically contextual substitutions and intact-group alternatives around amides, ethers, amines and sulfur centres. Generate alternatives from existing graphs and let accepted feedback establish their value; distinguish reactive N/O-halogen or peroxy connections from ordinary carbon-bound halogens, rather than treating all halogens or all N-S bonds alike.

transferable_gaps.evidence: One supplied stream has a median of 69 heavy atoms and reaches 120, with an 84-heavy-atom digest-best molecule, whereas other digest examples collapse to methane, acetylene or tiny halogen fragments with very low labels. Stronger compact molecules also exist. Molecular growth, chemical complexity and observed score therefore have different relationships across the supplied streams.
transferable_gaps.gap: The output lacks reliable control over both excessive fragment accumulation and destructive collapse of useful molecular cores.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Provide bounded core-preserving growth, contraction and connected-fragment replacement, with explicit attention to retained functional groups and molecular size. Learn which variants help from the current accepted molecular/score history, without fixing a universal preferred size or forcing either growth or pruning.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Every digest task has stereocentre_rate 0.0. Passive RDKit reading identifies unassigned tetrahedral centres in 2200 of 4350 generated child molecules, while finding no assigned tetrahedral centres or specified double-bond stereo. Cited examples include substituted cyclic amines, cyclobutenol, acetal-like carbons and substituted alkenes.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator produces stereogenic structures without demonstrated stereochemical resolution or coverage.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Represent and preserve existing stereochemical information through graph changes and provide bounded chemically feasible stereoisomer alternatives where new centres or alkene geometry arise. Their value remains a hypothesis to test using ordinary accepted feedback; an unspecified SMILES does not demonstrate exploration of all its stereoisomers.

transferable_gaps.evidence: All digest charged_rate values are 0.0, and all 4350 child proposal graphs have zero formal charge. Some of the strongest cited structures nevertheless contain cyclic amines, secondary amines and amidines; other abundant nitrogens are amide-like or aromatic. Neutral encoding therefore conceals chemically different ionisation possibilities.
transferable_gaps.gap: The output contains potentially ionisable motifs but demonstrates no explicit charge-state alternatives.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Distinguish nitrogen environments and support chemically valid state alternatives using only molecular structure, ordinary identity admission and accepted labels. Preserve clarity about the proposed chemical state; no particular charge, pKa or environmental protonation state follows from these observed scores alone.

transferable_gaps.evidence: The panel includes rich rings and multiple families, yet stronger digest examples repeatedly occupy substituted indole carboxamides, repeated carbonyl-bearing heteroaryls, aryl-linked N-rings and annulated dicarbonyl scaffolds. Several large, visibly different structures receive the same recorded label, and some seed families retain the parent's best identity. These observations do not support equating string novelty with new useful chemistry.
transferable_gaps.gap: Useful structural coverage remains uneven despite abundant rings and many distinct molecular strings.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Expand scaffold and ring-connection alternatives that preserve useful donor/acceptor arrangements at comparable size, alongside local substitutions. Assess coverage by molecular cores and intact functional groups, using accepted feedback to discover where a new topology matters; do not prescribe a benchmark-specific scaffold or assume that adding rings improves coverage.

method_name: Mol GA: rank-selected de novo graph evolution
method_thesis: Anchor the root in Mol GA: maintain a population of oracle-evaluated molecular graphs, sample breeding parents across high-ranked quantiles, generate new offspring through graph crossover and atom/bond mutations, and update survivors greedily after each observation. These are the proposal and selection mechanisms described by [Tripp and Hernández-Lobato (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.09267v1). Start from the supplied initial observations and incorporate newly evaluated offspring immediately, following the evaluator's announced batching. Repeated graph edits and recombination create an evolving search space; no corpus ranking, stored molecule library, pretrained model, or fixed candidate enumeration is needed. The causal hypothesis is that direct selection on task-local scores concentrates successive structural changes around improving molecules quickly enough to raise the final best observed score. The published evidence concerns a larger-budget AUC-Top-10 setting, so its transfer to this benchmark's final Top-1 objective remains a hypothesis.

retained_mechanisms: Task-local scored molecular-graph population with score-ranked parent sampling across three high-ranked quantiles.
Local atom/bond mutations with inherited inner retries and occasional multistep graph walks.

Direct formula-preserving C/N positional exchange within an eligible aromatic six-member ring, appended to the inherited uniformly sampled per-site replacement menu with ordinary aromaticity, checking and novelty gates.
Chemical sanitization and pool-only stable canonical identity admission, preserving the checked graph under admitted normalization and boundedly rejecting unresolved representations.
Bounded greedy score-ranked survival and breeding from accepted offspring, with a separate complete ordered accepted-score archive.
Task-local binary Morgan/Tanimoto Gaussian-process conditioning with unit amplitude, empirical score normalization, cached features and bounded Cholesky retries.
Correlated latent posterior draws over fresh surplus pools, sequential masked maximizers, feedback refitting, previous-emission probes and inherited explicit numerical fallback.
Accepted-archive marginal-likelihood observation-noise selection over the fixed seven-point ladder, with deterministic exact-tie ordering and reuse of the winning training factor and coefficients.

activation_observables.measurement: Reconstruct every Child fit from its exact earlier accepted archive, unchanged binary features/kernel, normalization, fixed ladder and actual jitter receipts. Independently calculate all seven standardized Gaussian log marginal likelihoods, audit the deterministic winner and compare with the inherited multiplier 1. Report selected multipliers by fit/task/seed, nonreference counts, evidence margins, boundary selections, constant-label states and changes after feedback. On identical archives and ordered pools reconstruct the fixed-noise Parent posterior and the selected-noise Child posterior; measure differences in training diagonal, coefficients, means, latent SDs and full conditional covariance using a 1e-12 numerical reporting threshold and magnitude distributions. Feature vectors and noiseless train/train, train/pool and pool/pool kernels must remain identical. A changed selected noise with corresponding implemented posterior changes establishes activation. Reference-scale winners or numerically coincident outputs are explicit no-change opportunities. Better training evidence is not prospective calibration evidence.
activation_observables.name: Reconstruct each fit from its ordered accepted training records and declared feature/kernel/normalization/noise settings; report changed representations, similarity relationships or posterior values only on eligible fixed-data comparisons.

activation_observables.measurement: Join each pre-feedback emitted prediction to the next fit on that identical molecule, excluding terminal observations without a later suggestion. Record before/after fit versions, selected noise and numerical jitter, normalization mean/scale, score-unit mean/SD and standardized latent variance. Compare each fit with a passive sigma0 model on the identical accepted state. Separate the changed fitted noise from archive growth and score-normalization changes; do not require raw SD to contract or widen monotonically over a changing archive. On a fixed archive larger selected noise should reduce the conditioning strength and cannot decrease conditional covariance in exact arithmetic; audit finite numerical discrepancies without attributing chronological changes solely to noise. Verify that pool and previous-emission probes use the same selected factor.
activation_observables.name: Compare pre-feedback predictions with the next fit on the identical emitted molecules, excluding terminal observations with no next suggestion; separate changes in normalization from changes in conditional uncertainty.

activation_observables.measurement: Use only actual scored emissions and their pre-feedback predictions to report chronological MSE, same-fit archive-mean baseline MSE, signed error, within-batch average-rank association, interval widths and empirical +/-1.96 latent-SD coverage by supplied task and seed. Report noise-inclusive coverage separately using the selected fit noise and score scale; changing the modeled noise is not proof that the oracle itself is noisy. finding_summary.headline: Learned noise improved selected-stream error and coverage, but mean search score fell 0.015961
finding_summary.insights: The experiment separates a real regularization benefit from a search benefit. The strongest controlled prediction improvement occurs in sitagliptin: latent coverage rises from 466 to 558 of 870 scored molecules, with lower MSE in all three seeds. DRD2 instead loses three covered molecules on the same scored identities, and ranking deteriorates in the pooled comparison. Thus reducing average prediction error and winning training likelihood do not establish better discrimination among the next candidates to evaluate. The frequent upper and lower boundary choices show that different accepted molecular/score relationships call for very different regularization; they leave the adequacy of the finite ladder unresolved. Substantial undercoverage remains even with learned noise, particularly in the harder streams. Scalar noise cannot distinguish molecules with identical binary fingerprints or correct every mismatch in the representation and mean model. The chemical assessment also finds recurring ring-rich families with more reactive N/O-halogen and peroxide motifs, oversized assemblies and unresolved stereochemistry, so these predictive gains supply no evidence that chemical liabilities were repaired. The measured same-data comparison supports a modest, heterogeneous prediction benefit. It cannot assign counterfactual scores to unselected molecules or identify which changed choices caused the loss in whole-search endpoints. The mechanism executed; the expected score improvement did not occur.
finding_summary.results: Noise selection changed the implemented posterior in 434 of 435 fits, and every likelihood winner and recorded evaluation choice reconstructed correctly. The smallest available noise won 179 fits and the largest won 116; the chosen scale changed after feedback at 41 of 420 opportunities. On the same earlier archives and the same 4350 subsequently scored molecules, prediction MSE fell from 0.0121771 with fixed noise to 0.0116233 with learned noise. Latent 95% interval coverage rose from 79.75% to 82.51%, while mean within-batch rank correlation fell from 0.41596 to 0.39609. Noise-inclusive coverage reached 89.91% with wider intervals, reported separately from latent uncertainty. The same random draws applied to the two distributions changed the selected molecule set in 255 of 435 batches. Despite those prediction gains, mean final-best score fell from 0.551771 to 0.535810, a paired change of -0.015961 against the registered +0.002 target; seed variability increased from 0.008223 to 0.023346. One seed macro improved and two declined. Task means rose for median and sitagliptin and slightly for decoration, but fell for DRD2 and zaleplon. All tasks completed their budgets, and every factorization succeeded at the first jitter.

finding_summary.headline: Learned noise improved selected-stream error and coverage, but mean search score fell 0.015961
finding_summary.insights: The experiment separates a real regularization benefit from a search benefit. The strongest controlled prediction improvement occurs in sitagliptin: latent coverage rises from 466 to 558 of 870 scored molecules, with lower MSE in all three seeds. DRD2 instead loses three covered molecules on the same scored identities, and ranking deteriorates in the pooled comparison. Thus reducing average prediction error and winning training likelihood do not establish better discrimination among the next candidates to evaluate. The frequent upper and lower boundary choices show that different accepted molecular/score relationships call for very different regularization; they leave the adequacy of the finite ladder unresolved. Substantial undercoverage remains even with learned noise, particularly in the harder streams. Scalar noise cannot distinguish molecules with identical binary fingerprints or correct every mismatch in the representation and mean model. The chemical assessment also finds recurring ring-rich families with more reactive N/O-halogen and peroxide motifs, oversized assemblies and unresolved stereochemistry, so these predictive gains supply no evidence that chemical liabilities were repaired. The measured same-data comparison supports a modest, heterogeneous prediction benefit. It cannot assign counterfactual scores to unselected molecules or identify which changed choices caused the loss in whole-search endpoints. The mechanism executed; the expected score improvement did not occur.
finding_summary.results: Noise selection changed the implemented posterior in 434 of 435 fits, and every likelihood winner and recorded evaluation choice reconstructed correctly. The smallest available noise won 179 fits and the largest won 116; the chosen scale changed after feedback at 41 of 420 opportunities. On the same earlier archives and the same 4350 subsequently scored molecules, prediction MSE fell from 0.0121771 with fixed noise to 0.0116233 with learned noise. Latent 95% interval coverage rose from 79.75% to 82.51%, while mean within-batch rank correlation fell from 0.41596 to 0.39609. Noise-inclusive coverage reached 89.91% with wider intervals, reported separately from latent uncertainty. The same random draws applied to the two distributions changed the selected molecule set in 255 of 435 batches. Despite those prediction gains, mean final-best score fell from 0.551771 to 0.535810, a paired change of -0.015961 against the registered +0.002 target; seed variability increased from 0.008223 to 0.023346. One seed macro improved and two declined. Task means rose for median and sitagliptin and slightly for decoration, but fell for DRD2 and zaleplon. All tasks completed their budgets, and every factorization succeeded at the first jitter.

finding_summary.headline: Learned noise improved selected-stream error and coverage, but mean search score fell 0.015961
finding_summary.insights: The experiment separates a real regularization benefit from a search benefit. The strongest controlled prediction improvement occurs in sitagliptin: latent coverage rises from 466 to 558 of 870 scored molecules, with lower MSE in all three seeds. DRD2 instead loses three covered molecules on the same scored identities, and ranking deteriorates in the pooled comparison. Thus reducing average prediction error and winning training likelihood do not establish better discrimination among the next candidates to evaluate. The frequent upper and lower boundary choices show that different accepted molecular/score relationships call for very different regularization; they leave the adequacy of the finite ladder unresolved. Substantial undercoverage remains even with learned noise, particularly in the harder streams. Scalar noise cannot distinguish molecules with identical binary fingerprints or correct every mismatch in the representation and mean model. The chemical assessment also finds recurring ring-rich families with more reactive N/O-halogen and peroxide motifs, oversized assemblies and unresolved stereochemistry, so these predictive gains supply no evidence that chemical liabilities were repaired. The measured same-data comparison supports a modest, heterogeneous prediction benefit. It cannot assign counterfactual scores to unselected molecules or identify which changed choices caused the loss in whole-search endpoints. The mechanism executed; the expected score improvement did not occur.
finding_summary.results: Noise selection changed the implemented posterior in 434 of 435 fits, and every likelihood winner and recorded evaluation choice reconstructed correctly. The smallest available noise won 179 fits and the largest won 116; the chosen scale changed after feedback at 41 of 420 opportunities. On the same earlier archives and the same 4350 subsequently scored molecules, prediction MSE fell from 0.0121771 with fixed noise to 0.0116233 with learned noise. Latent 95% interval coverage rose from 79.75% to 82.51%, while mean within-batch rank correlation fell from 0.41596 to 0.39609. Noise-inclusive coverage reached 89.91% with wider intervals, reported separately from latent uncertainty. The same random draws applied to the two distributions changed the selected molecule set in 255 of 435 batches. Despite those prediction gains, mean final-best score fell from 0.551771 to 0.535810, a paired change of -0.015961 against the registered +0.002 target; seed variability increased from 0.008223 to 0.023346. One seed macro improved and two declined. Task means rose for median and sitagliptin and slightly for decoration, but fell for DRD2 and zaleplon. All tasks completed their budgets, and every factorization succeeded at the first jitter.

molecular_assessment.headline: Ring-rich molecules retain reactive substituents, oversized assemblies and unresolved stereochemistry
molecular_assessment.overall_character: This assessment covers every supplied trajectory for node n-9002c3d22369 and parent n-9edaa26007c3: all five objectives and seeds 0, 1 and 2, with 900 observations and 870 optimizer proposals per objective in each node. The digest's tasks_without_trajectories list is empty. Its initial excerpt represents seed 0 and its final excerpt represents seed 2; the full trajectories were read to cover the other seeds. The molecules contain abundant phenyl and aza-aromatic rings, fused and bridged heterocycles, carbonyl groups, ethers, amines and halogens. Different seeds retain different families, including indole carboxamides, thiocarbonyl-linked pyrazoles, repeated carbonyl-bearing heteroaryls, aryl-linked cyclic amines and annulated dicarbonyl heterocycles. Structural diversity is moderate across the panel but uneven within the stronger examples. SMILES uniqueness alone would overstate chemically useful diversity. The digest's ring-closure rates range from 0.9609 to 0.9908 and aromatic-token presence rates from 0.9460 to 0.9908; these are fractions of proposal strings, not atom fractions or perceived ring counts. Passive RDKit 2023.09.6 parsing succeeds for all 4350 generated records per node. The child has a median of 31 heavy atoms, 5 perceived rings and 3 aromatic rings; the parent has 30, 5 and 3. Child N-halogen-bearing, O-halogen-bearing and O-O-bearing molecule counts are 870, 375 and 161, compared with 667, 319 and 85 in the parent. These structural alerts require chemical context: a valid graph is not a synthesis or stability demonstration, and an N-S bond by itself is not an objection. Some conventional aromatic amides and amine scaffolds look tractable, but the repeated reactive groups and large or unusually connected ring systems make overall synthetic plausibility questionable and drug-likeness weak. Every generated SMILES is formally uncharged and lacks specified tetrahedral or double-bond stereochemistry; RDKit identifies unassigned tetrahedral centres in 2200 child molecules. Basic amines nevertheless occur prominently, so the charge encoding does not establish solution-state neutrality. All score statements below reuse observed labels; no new molecular scoring, activation judgement, synthesis calculation or target-specific pharmacophore inference was performed. Numeric graph descriptions, full file hashes and seed comparisons are reproducible from /projects/standard/adeshwal/shared/zhou2577/SPIRAL/runs/SPIRAL2/policy/responses/r0011-08-improve-L01-molecular-audit.json and its adjacent passive audit script.
